item.title: Ground Stop Highlights Chronic Vulnerabilities in Air Traffic System
item.description:
The nationwide ground stop that brought air travel across the country to a halt Friday evening has highlighted persistent weaknesses in the Federal Aviation Administration’s aging air traffic control infrastructure that has had several disruptive failures in recent months.

Officials called the rare ground stop after outdated communications lines became overloaded and began to fail, interrupting communication lines between air traffic controllers and pilots, according to Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy and Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin.

The breakdown occurred less than two months after a circuit failure and severed fiber optic cable caused crippling ground stops and delays at airports along the East Coast. Smaller outages unfolded in October at Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina and George Bush International Airport in Houston, when contractors accidentally cut into fiber line.

The Friday ground stop, which was only the third the F.A.A. has issued this century, eclipsed the fallout of previous air traffic communications equipment failures. The F.A.A. has yet to identify precisely what caused communication lines to falter.

But the successive episodes have underscored the structural vulnerabilities that continue to hamper air traffic controllers’ ability to safely manage flight traffic, even after concerted efforts to make improvements. And they raised questions about whether the federal authorities have done enough to create backup systems and redundancies to prevent disruptive or even catastrophic failures.

For decades, the air traffic communications have relied on a system that runs on analog copper wire, floppy disks and alphabetical keyboards so old that the F.A.A. has difficulty sourcing spare parts. Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion in funding to help pay for upgrades, after a series of outages in an air traffic control facilities, including the one serving Newark Liberty International Airport, caused alarming losses of radar and other communications capabilities.

Earlier this month, L3 Harris, the primary telecoms contractor tasked to manage the system upgrades, boasted on its website that it had converted about 70 percent of the copper line to fiber optic cable; last week, the F.A.A. announced it would begin to phase out floppy disks.

But the disruptions in recent weeks showed that those upgrades had serious vulnerabilities themselves.

In September, when a circuit at a regional air traffic facility failed, operators had no backup options beyond the fiber line, 600 feet of which they discovered — to their surprise — had been severed by a construction crew in New Jersey working on Amtrak project. More than 430 flights were canceled before the system was fixed several hours later.

A similar incident occurred in October at the Raleigh-Durham International Airport in North Carolina, when a contractor working on plumbing accidentally severed a fiber line. The airport was forced to issue a ground stop for several hours. Just one day after that, officials were forced to issue a ground stop at George Bush International Airport, when yet another contractor inadvertently severed a fiber line.

The fiber line upgrades themselves, Mr. Bedford told reporters at the time, were not enough to save the system from failure.

Ideally, the F.A.A. wanted to put data into cloud services, he told reporters then, so that “when you have a fiber cut, you have multiple pathways of backup.”

“Today we have physical fiber and when it’s cut, there’s one redundancy, and when we lose that, there’s no more redundancy,” he added.

Friday’s national ground stop revealed that the lack of redundancies in the F.A.A.’s system could trigger catastrophic failures in other ways and touched off a blame game in Washington. Mr. Duffy seized on the chaos to hammer Congress, saying it had failed to pony up enough funding to pay for systemwide upgrades.

“How many more times does this have to happen for Congress to give the money to fix it?” he told reporters at the White House Friday night, asking that lawmakers approve $50 billion in emergency funds for the project. Their lack of action, he said, had forced his department to pursue patchwork upgrades that were insufficient. It was a dramatic increase in his demand for additional money, which for the past several months has hovered at $30 billion.

But lawmakers in both parties are raising questions about how efficiently Mr. Duffy and the F.A.A. have been spending the money they have already been given.

“Today’s unprecedented breakdown is the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents under the Trump administration’s failed leadership,” Representative Hakeem Jeffries, the minority leader, said in a statement issued shortly after Mr. Duffy’s news conference, accusing the administration of failing to take responsibility for its failures in “the latest in a series of unacceptable air travel incidents.”

item.title: Here’s Why It Could Take Days for Flights to Return to Normal
item.description:
The near-total shutdown of the nation’s airspace ended on Friday evening, but its ripple effects continued into Saturday as airlines canceled thousands of flights.

By Saturday morning, almost 15 percent of the day’s flights had been scrapped, and the number was still climbing. The recovery will most likely last for days as airlines work to juggle their schedules, rebook passengers and reposition planes.

Aviation functions like a relay race. To work well, many things have to align in the same place at the same time, including the availability of planes, crews and an open airport gate.

On Friday, thousands of planes were pulled from the air, filling up limited space on the ground. Many returned to the airports they had just left, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm. Jets at crowded airports weren’t allowed to depart and sat idle while flight crews quickly hit their legal working limits.

Pilots are generally limited to eight or nine hours of flying and a total shift length of 9 to 14 hours, though union contracts and airline policies often shrink those windows. Flight attendants are also governed by limits on the length of their shift. Both must receive lengthy breaks in between shifts, too.

For instance, a pilot who was scheduled to fly from New York to Miami on Friday night could easily have timed out while waiting for the ground stop to end. That would have left the airline struggling to find replacement pilots not only for the flight from New York, but also for the flight that pilot was scheduled to operate out of Miami on Saturday. Multiply that by hundreds and airline schedules can quickly implode.

Take N865DN, the tail number for a Boeing 737 operated by Delta Air Lines. It started Friday flying from Charleston, S.C., to Atlanta. From there, it made round trip flights to Louisville, Ky., and Norfolk, Va., returning to Atlanta, according to Flightradar24, a flight-tracking service.

The plane was supposed to fly on to Savannah, Ga., back to Atlanta, and then to Chicago, where it would start the day on Saturday. But it never made those last three flights.

Delta rebuilt its Saturday plan, with the plane scheduled to fly from Atlanta to Spokane, Wash., and on to Salt Lake City and Raleigh-Durham, N.C.

For minor disruptions, airlines can play catch-up by restarting flights and trying to make up for lost time. But bigger disruptions, such as the one that occurred Friday, often require resetting the network by proactively canceling many flights.

item.title: Key Witness in Comey Case Attests to Justice Dept.’s Aggressive Tactics
item.description:
For more than a year, the Justice Department has gone hard after James B. Comey, the former F.B.I. director, using an array of rule-bending tactics in an effort to satisfy President Trump’s drive to see him charged.

In the three cases filed against Mr. Comey so far, prosecutors have improperly used search warrants to get evidence, made glaring errors in front of a grand jury and enlisted a mafia hit man in an effort to prove that Mr. Comey had broken the law.

They also considered treating The New York Times as Mr. Comey’s co-conspirator in a leak prosecution in what appeared to be a bid to breathe new life into accusations that might otherwise have been barred by the statute of limitations.

On Friday night, a new court filing added additional details to a portrait of belligerence, showing just how far investigators have been willing to roam in their pursuit of Mr. Comey.

This summer, the filing said, prosecutors hauled two workers at a New York apartment building in front of a grand jury in Florida after they refused to let an F.B.I. agent inside to serve a subpoena on one of its residents — a longtime confidant of Mr. Comey’s from whom the government wanted testimony.

The prosecutors also threatened to charge the confidant, Daniel C. Richman, with obstruction of justice for supposedly evading the subpoena, though he says that his lawyers had already agreed to accept it on his behalf.

The new documents, filed by Mr. Richman in Federal District Court in Washington, were nominally intended to support an effort by CNN to persuade a judge to unseal secret filings that the Justice Department has submitted over the past several months in a case related to the Comey prosecutions.

But the filing amounted to a bill of particulars, laying out the ways in which Mr. Richman and his lawyers believe that the Trump administration has badgered him as it continued to pursue Mr. Comey.

“Recent actions by the government suggest that the government’s interest in the covered materials is not related to a viable investigation but instead part of a harassment campaign, which undermines any law enforcement interest the government may have in sealing,” his lawyers wrote.

The Justice Department did not respond to a message seeking comment.

Mr. Richman, an Ivy League law professor who served as an aide to Mr. Comey at the F.B.I., has been at the center of a number of investigations into Mr. Comey reaching back to Mr. Trump’s first term in the White House. Prosecutors have repeatedly sought to build a case that he and Mr. Comey broke the law by working together to release information to the news media about sensitive investigations.

Most recently, Mr. Richman was summoned in September to appear in front of a grand jury in Florida where prosecutors are working on the so-called grand conspiracy case. That investigation is based on the far-fetched theory that the criminal inquiries into Mr. Trump over the past decade or so — including some that Mr. Comey worked on — were part of a single plot to sink his political prospects.

The grand conspiracy case has been marred from the outset by a lack of focus and a wave of firings and resignations of the prosecutors in charge of it. And Mr. Richman’s new court filing bolstered the picture of an investigation steeped in chaos.

The papers described “a series of unsettling and irregular communications” in which three prosecutors gave Mr. Richman different answers to the question of whether he was a target or merely a subject of the inquiry.

They also indicated that prosecutors could not quite agree about whether to grant Mr. Richman immunity before he appeared before the grand jury. Mr. Richman ultimately invoked his Fifth Amendment right against self-incrimination.

This description of prosecutors reaching for hardball tactics but fumbling at times to enact them was in keeping with the way in which the Justice Department has behaved in other cases focused on Mr. Comey.

In the first indictment filed against him, in which he was accused of lying to Congress about his dealings with the news media, prosecutors bent — and sometimes broke — the normal rules of criminal procedure. In that case, filed in Federal District Court in Alexandria, Va., three judges took issue with the Justice Department’s conduct.

One judge determined that investigators had unlawfully obtained a critical trove of evidence in the case — namely, a cache of messages exchanged by Mr. Comey and Mr. Richman — by reusing a search warrant they initially secured in a different case. Another judge found that the inexperienced prosecutor picked by Mr. Trump to bring the charges made several mistakes while presenting the case to a grand jury.

Ultimately, a third judge threw out the case after ruling that the prosecutor, Lindsey Halligan, who had once worked as Mr. Trump’s personal lawyer, had been improperly appointed to her prosecutorial post.

The second case against Mr. Comey, filed in the Eastern District of North Carolina, was similarly marked by an unusual working theory and unorthodox investigative tactics. It centered on accusations that Mr. Comey threatened Mr. Trump’s life by posting a photograph of seashells on a beach arranged to read, “86 47.” Prosecutors claim that the image showed Mr. Comey’s desire to “86” — or kill — Mr. Trump, who is the 47th president.

In seeking to prove this allegation, investigators interviewed Salvatore Gravano, a former mafia hit man. The investigators wanted Mr. Gravano’s help in making the case that Mr. Comey, who worked on mob cases when he was a young federal prosecutor, would have known that “86” was mafia slang for killing.

The third case against Mr. Comey accuses him of authorizing the release of national security information in October 2016 that prosecutors said appeared in an article in The New York Times.

Those charges were filed in a highly unusual manner, laid out in a document known as a criminal information, which can be brought by prosecutors alone without the immediate approval of either a judge or a grand jury.

Prosecutors filed the information in Washington exactly a decade after the publication of a Times article that exposed the novel use of a surveillance technique on the email platform Yahoo. Mr. Comey’s lawyers have accused the government of improperly using the information to skirt the 10-year statute of limitations in the case and have asked a federal judge to dismiss it.

But prosecutors have raised the possibility of adding additional defendants — including Mr. Richman or potentially The Times — to the case in a way that could extend the statute of limitations past October.

item.title: Repair That Triggered Air Traffic Meltdown Was Expected to be ‘Routine’
item.description:
The communications failures that prompted Federal Aviation Administration officials to issue a nationwide ground stop started when L3 Harris, a contractor managing the agency’s telecoms network, made a standard upgrade at a remote air traffic location, federal officials said Saturday.

The contractor was conducting work on Friday that was needed to replace aging analog copper wire with more modern fiber optic cable, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, told reporters. The “routine” task was being done at a location remote and small enough that officials assumed a Friday afternoon upgrade would pose no meaningful disruption to the air traffic, he said.

That presumption proved wrong, as the changeover from copper to fiber started flooding the system with levels of data it could not handle, triggering a cascade of communications failures across the air traffic facilities that manage the national air space. Officials, alarmed at the scope of the problems, decided to issue a rare nationwide ground stop for hours.

As of Saturday morning, administration officials still have not determined whether L3 Harris or shoddy equipment was at fault.

“What we’re working to determine was whether we had incompetence, meaning it was user error or installer error from L3 Harris, or did they install a faulty router?” Mr. Duffy told reporters. “We haven’t determined what the fault was.”

Representatives for L3 Harris did not immediately return email and phone requests for comment on Saturday.

L3 Harris has been managing the F.A.A.’s effort to shift its antiquated communications system of analog copper lines to a nationwide network of fiber optic cable. Earlier this month, the company boasted that they had completed such upgrades at 70 percent of air traffic control facilities, a figure that F.A.A. administrator Bryan Bedford echoed at Saturday’s news conference.

Such upgrades — which Mr. Bedford characterized as “sustainment,” not modernization — are vital to ensure that the air traffic control system can operate safely, he and Mr. Duffy told reporters.

Officials were sure, Mr. Duffy said, that they had identified the origin of the problem; for instance, when they isolated the location and took it offline, the system’s functionality was restored. There was no evidence that nefarious activity, or the agency’s recent efforts to outfit its air traffic control facilities with assistive A.I. technology, had played a role in triggering Friday’s problems, he and Mr. Bedford added.

But the episode raises serious questions about how well the F.A.A. understands the potential vulnerabilities of their existing network as it makes patches and upgrades to antiquated technology.

The routers in air traffic control facilities, which became overloaded with over 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds, were mostly manufactured in 2001, Mr. Duffy said, and were out of service by 2006.

“Was it a faulty installation? Was it a faulty configuration? Or was it just a bad piece of faulty technology?” Mr. Bedford said, without offering a conclusion.

He added that officials would have to reassess their protocols, and “pivot” in the future to avoid causing similar sweeping problems when upgrading equipment.

item.title: Travel Nightmare Continues for Stranded Passengers Awaiting Flights
item.description:
Travelers across the United States on Saturday morning were still feeling the frustrating, plan-ruining aftershocks of the ground stop that halted air travel for hours on Friday.

“I’ve been right here for 20 hours,” said Jasmine Harp, a passenger at Kennedy International Airport in New York. “I have not showered, I have not slept. It’s torture.”

Ms. Harp, 25, was going on 48 hours of travel, trying to get home to Detroit after spending a week in Paris for her birthday.

She had just sat down in her airplane seat on Friday when the pilot told passengers to deplane. A few hours later, the flight was canceled. She described a mad dash to the baggage claim, where passengers worked to secure their luggage.

“They just dumped everybody’s bags off all at once,” she said. “It was chaotic.”

To make matters worse, Ms. Harp had left the gate area but still had to wait for her rebooked flight, which was to depart at 3 p.m. the next day. That meant no restaurants, no shops and, most uncomfortably, no seats. She found a luggage counter to perch on.

“I wish they would let me in the lounge,” she said Saturday morning, as she broke out some trail mix that she had rationed throughout the night.

Antonio Alemán, 39, whose transfer to Lima, Peru was canceled late on Friday, spent an uncomfortable night at the same airport. The airline, Latam, rebooked him on a flight for Tuesday. “I don’t know where I will stay until then,” he said.

Further south, the scene at Hartsfield-Jackson Atlanta International Airport looked, at first glance, as if it might have been a typical Saturday morning, with passengers checking bags and waiting at security checkpoints.

A closer inspection, however, revealed travelers sleeping in the airport’s quiet corners, departure screens speckled with cancellation and delay notices, and backups at customer service desks.

Barefoot and sprawled out on the carpeted floor in Hartsfield-Jackson’s central atrium, Glory Agunbiade, 16, and her mother, Itanola Agunbiade, 56, had managed to steal four or five hours of sleep after their Friday flight to Indianapolis was canceled.

From their makeshift campsite — they each used their bags as pillows — the pair bickered over how the federal government had handled Friday’s ground stop. While the elder Ms. Agunbiade saw the decision to halt flights as a necessary precaution and said it was “not anybody’s fault,” her teenage daughter was more frustrated.

“It’s like all we know is that the problem was about communication,” the younger Ms. Agunbiade said. “I feel like we’re entitled to more information.”

In Chicago, Pedro and Aorbys Vasquez were resting at O’Hare International Airport on Saturday, more than 12 hours after their connecting flight to Paris was supposed to leave. Their original flight was delayed six times before it was finally canceled. By that point, they could not find an available hotel room.

The couple slept in seats with nothing more than neck pillows to comfort them. Their new flight is scheduled for 6:45 p.m., 24 hours after they were originally scheduled to depart.

Looking at the bright side of an experience he called exhausting, Vasquez joked, “at least we shouldn’t have a problem sleeping on our flight.”

Robert Chiarito and Sean Keenan contributed reporting.

item.title: Democrats push back on Duffy’s demand for $50 billion to upgrade air traffic systems.
item.description:
Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, on Friday requested $50 billion for a “complete overhaul” of the aging air traffic control system, laying much of the blame on Congress after flights across the nation were halted for hours.

Mr. Duffy’s demand thrust the funding issue to the forefront of the final days of Republican control on Capitol Hill.

Speaker Mike Johnson told Fox News on Saturday morning that he would seek to add more funding for the Federal Aviation Administration into an “aggressive legislative package” he planned to put forth in the lame-duck session of Congress.

Democrats said the Trump administration had plenty of money it could put toward improving an outdated air traffic control system — funds it was using instead for Immigration and Customs Enforcement. They said Congress needed to begin investigating the failures of the Trump administration.

Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion to help pay for upgrades to the air traffic communications system. Republican lawmakers have introduced the Modern Skies Act in the House and Senate, a bill that would authorize another $30 billion in upgrades.

That bill seeks to allocate $10.1 billon for air traffic control modernization, $10 billion for control towers and airport improvements, and another $10 billion for an aging terminal pilot program.

But the bill has no Democratic co-sponsors. And on Friday night, Democrats said the airport crisis was caused by how the Trump administration had allocated money and overseen the F.A.A.

Senator Chuck Schumer, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, said that Mr. Duffy’s request for another $50 billion was alarming, given that Republicans had “showered ICE with billions in funding.”

He added that “if this administration is serious about aviation safety, it should stop making excuses and work with Congress to put taxpayer dollars where they’re actually needed.”

Representative Hakeem Jeffries, Democrat of New York and the minority leader, blamed the breakdown on the Trump administration.

“From Day 1, instead of taking responsibility, MAGA extremists have fired and scapegoated hard-working federal employees whose job it is to keep our skies safe, particularly women and people of color,” he said.

House Democrats promised an investigation next year into how air traffic was brought to a standstill. “Preserve all documents and emails,” Democrats on the committee overseeing homeland security and the Transportation Security Administration wrote online. “Oversight is coming.”

Senator Tammy Duckworth of Illinois, the senior Democrat on the subcommittee overseeing aviation, demanded a thorough investigation into the F.A.A.

Mr. Johnson, however, said that “we don’t really need any investigation to understand we need further investment.”

At a news conference on Friday night, Mr. Duffy said the issues were not partisan.

“It’s not Democrat, it’s not Republican. It’s American,” he said. “Give us the money to fix it.”

item.title: Defense Contractor L3Harris Was Behind Upgrade That Led to Ground Stop
item.description:
The hourslong halt to departing flights across the country on Friday started with routine maintenance on air traffic control equipment at a remote site, federal officials said on Saturday.

That work was being carried out by L3Harris Technologies, a little-known defense contractor that owns and operates essential communications infrastructure used by the Federal Aviation Administration.

Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy stopped short of saying that the company was at fault, but he vowed to investigate whether it bears responsibility.

“What did L3Harris do? Did they make mistakes yesterday?” he said at a news conference on Saturday. “They own this network. They’re our prime contractor. I can’t go somewhere else. They own it. Or was it a faulty router? And we’re going to find that out. And frankly, we’re going to hold people accountable.”

In a statement on Saturday, L3Harris said that it was supporting the F.A.A. investigation into what had happened and that it “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

The company was formed in 2019, the result of a merger of two defense contractors. It employed about 45,000 people at the start of this year and is based in Florida.

About 75 percent of its revenue comes from U.S. government contracts, many of them for the military. In 2025, the company was selected to retrofit a Boeing 747 donated by Qatar to be used as the interim Air Force One. L3Harris has generated more than $1 billion in annual profits since 2020.

The company also does a lot of work for the F.A.A., including maintaining networks that facilitate communications between air traffic controllers and pilots and receive plane location signals.

L3Harris owns the equipment used to transmit voice communications and data to and from air traffic control facilities, remote radar sites and weather stations, a network known as the F.A.A. Telecommunications Infrastructure. The company is in the midst of upgrading the copper wires used in that network to high-speed fiber optic cable across more than 4,400 sites, with over 70 percent of those lines already replaced.

Federal officials said on Saturday that they had halted departing flights a day earlier because of a communications disruption set off by a copper-to-fiber upgrade at a remote site, which they did not identify. A newly installed router began firing more than a thousand connection requests every few seconds, which disrupted voice communications and radar feeds. Ultimately, it took technicians 45 minutes to identify the problem.

The F.A.A. is trying to build a modern replacement to its telecommunications network with other partners, including AT&T and Verizon, over the next few years, Secretary Duffy said on Saturday. “Until I can build that, I’m stuck with L3Harris,” he said.

item.title: As Crisis Circled the Skies, Trump Kept Out of Sight and Off Topic
item.description:
With flights grounded for nearly five hours Friday evening, Americans heard from the homeland security secretary. They heard from the transportation secretary. They did not hear from President Trump.

At least not about the nationwide ground stop, the first major crisis the federal government has faced since the midterm elections. The halt grounded or delayed some 10,000 flights from coast to coast and confirmed what experts have been warning for years: that the nation’s flight safety system is perilously fragile.

Instead, the president, who remained behind the scenes at the White House, posted messages to social media that night on other topics.

“MAKE OUR ENTERTAINMENT INDUSTRY GREAT AGAIN!” he wrote on Truth Social, in the middle of the crisis, calling for tax incentives to lure movie production back to the United States.

The absence of Mr. Trump, who has made few public appearances since Democrats swept the midterms, seemed notable enough that Markwayne Mullin, the homeland security secretary, sought to assure the nation in the heat of the crisis on Friday night that the president was fully engaged, if not in his more common spot in front of the cameras.

“This is what President Trump does,” Mr. Mullin said in a news conference. “He puts leaders in place, and he allows them to lead. They even ask, you know, why is the president not talking? It’s because he’s allowed Secretary Duffy and us to go out there and explain to you what took place.” He was referring to Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, who appeared beside Mr. Mullin on Friday night.

By Saturday morning, Mr. Trump still hadn’t commented on the ground stop. Instead, he began attacking Gov. Gavin Newsom of California, a Democrat and political rival, over his commutation of death penalty sentences for more than 500 inmates, an action the governor took more than a week ago.

It is an old strategy in politics to let underlings be the bearers of bad news. Mr. Trump’s decision not to engage in public on a crisis with cascading effects across the country comes as Democrats in Congress have already vowed to investigate the administration’s handling of the shutdown.

With Mr. Trump steering clear of the topic on Friday night, Mr. Mullin and Mr. Duffy appeared at times to contradict each other as they tried to explain the breakdown that affected tens of thousands of people.

Transportation Department officials, in particular, were caught off guard when Mr. Mullin told reporters that the meltdown had occurred because new technology upgrades had “overwhelmed the older system,” according to two people familiar with the matter.

At the time, department officials had not made a determination of what precisely had overloaded the antiquated system and caused the meltdown to spiral across the country. Mr. Duffy also tried to gently redirect after Mr. Mullin’s remarks, stressing that old equipment, not new technology, was what had overloaded and failed. On Saturday, Mr. Duffy told reporters that a routine router replacement in a remote area had triggered the nationwide outages but officials could not yet say whether it had been because of a faulty part or a contractor error.

In a statement on Saturday, Mr. Duffy said: “We’re deeply grateful for Secretary Mullin and his team’s partnership as we worked through this challenging time.”

When asked where Mr. Trump was during the ground stop, the officials defended the president and heaped praise on him.

“Well, the two of us have talked to him,” Mr. Duffy said. “He’s in. I’ve talked to him on the phone. I’ve talked to him in the Oval. So has Markwayne.”

As the agency leaders addressed the media, Stephen Miller, the newly installed White House chief of staff, and Steven Cheung, the communications director, watched off to the side.

Asked for comment, the White House referred to the comments of Mr. Duffy and Mr. Mullin.

Mr. Duffy said Congress was to blame for the ground stop because the legislative branch had failed to fund updated technology for the Federal Aviation Administration. Lawmakers have privately questioned how efficiently the F.A.A. has spent money already appropriated, congressional aides say, and Democrats say the administration has prioritized issues like deportations over air safety.

“I want $50 billion,” Mr. Duffy said. “President Trump is a builder. He’s going to build this network and deliver for the American people.”

He added: “And when Secretary Duffy said he’s the greatest president we’ve had. You’ve never had a builder and a leader like President Trump lead this nation, have a vision and put the team together.”

Ever since Republicans were routed in the midterm elections, Mr. Trump has been keeping somewhat of a lower profile. Before the midterms, he embarked on a blitz of rallies across the country in which he spoke to the public nearly every night.

This week, he appeared in public sparingly: once at an impromptu appearance with the U.F.C. president Dana White as a follow-up to a post that Mr. Trump acknowledged was an attempt to distract from bad news cycles, and at a speech on Veterans Day.

Former Representative Marjorie Taylor Greene, Republican of Georgia, who was once a close ally of the president’s, noted that Mr. Trump has never been shy in putting his full focus on his construction projects, such as the attempted repairs to the Lincoln Memorial Reflecting Pool. But she noted that he seemed unengaged during the F.A.A. crisis.

“Trump constantly railed about fixing the reflection pool so much that he used the last day before massively losing the midterms to give a speech in front of the reflection pool bragging about he fixed the reflection pool,” she wrote on social media. But in a crisis that led to Mr. Duffy’s call for billions to upgrade air traffic systems, she wrote, “President Trump doesn’t even issue so much as a Truth Social post.”

She added: “While everyone was freaking out thinking we are under some sort of attack, Trump didn’t even bother to address the nation.”

On Saturday afternoon, Mr. Trump finally publicly acknowledged the matter, but only obliquely and through another’s words. He posted a quote attributed to Senator John Kennedy, Republican of Louisiana, that appeared to reference a desire for more funding for the F.A.A.: “The FAA Funding should be a stand alone Bill — We should get Democrat support for that!”

With the crisis largely over, though with many flights still canceled and disruption rife, the president posted again about the need for tax credits for the movie industry.

Maggie Haberman, Karoun Demirjian and Kate Kelly contributed reporting.

item.title: Stranded by planes, travelers turned to trains and automobiles.
item.description:
With more than 9,000 flights in the United States canceled Friday and 5,000 more shelved on Saturday, some travelers decided to take matters into their own hands by booking trains, cars and even moving vans.

But those attempts weren’t without frustration. Flooded by a surge, Amtrak’s website and app were both down on Friday, causing many travelers to have issues booking train travel.

Amtrak did not confirm the booking outages, but a spokesman said that the rail company was “seeing increased demand for travel across our network.”

The race to nab a rental car was competitive, with long lines at airport rental car counters and scarce inventory on online travel apps. At Hartsfield-Jackson International Airport and O’Hare International Airport, rental car companies including Hertz, Enterprise and Avis, turned away customers to wanted to rent cars for one-way trips. And some travelers said that rental car companies didn’t honor their reservations.

On Saturday morning, Hunter Cavell, 39, arrived at an Enterprise car rental location in the University Heights neighborhood of Washington after his flight to Jacksonville, Fla., was canceled Friday. He found a line of disgruntled customers who, like him, had reservations. There were no cars available.

Jessica Whitney was returning to Los Angeles from a work trip in Las Vegas Friday afternoon when the government grounded air traffic. Watching her Delta flight get delayed every half-hour, she and her co-worker decided to rent a car instead of waiting for their flight to get canceled. When she opened her company’s corporate travel booking app, there was one rental car nearby. She pounced to book it, but it was already gone.

So for $281, she booked a U-Haul truck, the kind people typically use when they are moving homes.

“The U-Haul agent thought it was hilarious,” said Ms. Whitney, 32. With their bags still stuck in Las Vegas, the back of the truck was empty. The duo spent the more than four-hour car ride home listening to the radio and gazing at the desert.

“It was better than staying in Vegas for another night for sure,” Ms. Whitney said. “When you’re at the end of a Vegas trip, you don’t want to stay another night.”

Other travelers with less flexibility opted to hire drivers.

Their flight to Jacksonville canceled, longtime friends Ann Bruns, 79, and Janice Simpson, 78, hired a driver to take them on the six-hour trip from Atlanta to Amelia Island in Florida, where they hoped to catch a cruise ship setting sail on Sunday.

Their luggage had already been loaded onto the plane bound for Jacksonville, and it was anyone’s guess when it might arrive. “We’re about to go on a cruise ship with no clothes,” Ms. Simpson said.

Other travelers said they had spent hours refreshing Amtrak’s app and website to grab spots on trains. After Claudia Davis’s flight from Ronald Reagan Washington National Airport to LaGuardia Airport was canceled Friday afternoon, she decided having an airline A.I. agent rebook her travel wasn’t worth the hassle. But booking a seat on a train home to New York took her until 2 a.m. and involved many error messages and an hourlong wait to reach an Amtrak representative by phone.

“I knew that since I was in a big city that there were so many ways to get home,” said Ms. Davis, 56, who lives in Manhattan. “I wouldn’t roll the dice after what happened yesterday in getting a new plane reservation.”

Though the three-and-a-half-hour train ride is more than double the flight time from Washington to New York, Ms. Davis said she had no real complaints. She whizzed by Newark’s airport.

item.title: After Her Baby Was Buried Alive, a Mother’s Painful Question: Why?
item.description:
The detectives dug quickly but carefully, as the baby’s cries underneath the freshly packed dirt grew louder.

Koah Sharp, just shy of his first birthday, had been buried alive for about 24 hours in Lexington County, S.C., the authorities said, entombed in a dog crate wrapped with a dirt-smeared towel. Deputies unearthed the 11-month-old on Tuesday, amazed to find him breathing.

On Friday evening Koah was in the arms of his 25-year-old pregnant mother, Dezarae Sharp, who was still trying to make sense of what had happened to her boy as she caressed his plump baby cheeks again.

“I can’t believe it still,” Ms. Sharp said in the first interview she has granted since her child, who is expected to fully recover, went missing. “It’s something you would see in a movie. It’s something you would see on TV. And the fact that it happened to him — I don’t know.”

Michael Comer, Koah’s father and Ms. Sharp’s ex-boyfriend, was arrested and charged with attempted murder, unlawful conduct toward a child, custodial interference and burglary.

“I didn’t think he could go that far,” Ms. Sharp said.

Koah’s disappearance and his remarkable survival have shocked people well beyond Lexington County, a booming manufacturing hub that is part suburbia, part rural and near the capital city of Columbia.

The authorities have not fully explained the events that led to Koah’s being buried in the woods, citing an ongoing investigation, nor have they explained how they pinpointed the patch of earth dusted with pine needles where they found Koah.

But interviews with Ms. Sharp, Mr. Comer’s father and former neighbors, as well as a review of court records and text messages, offer some clues. In recent weeks, Mr. Comer, 25, had drunk excessively, refused to take medication for schizophrenia disorder and complained about being separated from his ex and their son, according to his family, Ms. Sharp and recent texts.

Mr. Comer could not be reached for comment, and he did not have a lawyer as of Friday. His mother and his lawyer from a previous case did not respond to interview requests.

Ms. Sharp said she had known Mr. Comer since elementary school. They didn’t date until August 2024 but were friendly throughout their youth. Once in middle school, when a classmate put an arm around Ms. Sharp’s neck, Mr. Comer “got up to do something about it,” she recalled.

“He’s tried to protect me before,” Ms. Sharp said, as Koah, whose teeth were coming in, watched television, full off the fries he had nibbled. “It’s really shocking.”

Before Koah was born in December, Mr. Comer seemed “nervous but excited” to be a father, Ms. Sharp said. At the time, he worked at McDonald’s and at a US Foods distribution center. The pair lived in a peach-tinted, sun-faded mobile home they rented for about $850 a month.

Candace Akers, their neighbor, did not know them well but said she recalled seeing Ms. Sharp appearing very pregnant, with hair dyed blue. Ms. Akers said her only interaction with Mr. Comer this year had occurred while walking her dog near his lot; he knocked on the window and waved his hands, telling her to get lost.

Parenting went fine at first, but in May, Ms. Sharp said, she confronted Mr. Comer about pornography she had discovered on his phone, something they had argued about before.

Afterward, Mr. Comer tripped and kicked her, Ms. Sharp said. Then, he shoved her against a dryer as she held Koah in her arms, according to Ms. Sharp and court records.

In the moment, Mr. Sharp said, he told her that he was unaware she had been holding Koah. She called the police, which led the State Department of Social Services to get involved. Ms. Sharp broke up with Mr. Comer, who pleaded guilty to a domestic violence charge, and moved away, she said.

Mr. Comer also pleaded guilty to an aggravated breach of peace charge related to a separate altercation with a different person in July, according to court records and Ms. Sharp.

As a result of that charge, Mr. Comer served a few months in jail. When he was released, his estranged father, John Comer, said he picked him up and offered to help put his son’s life back together, proposing that he move into his house in rural Batesburg-Leesville. John Comer and Ms. Sharp both said that Mr. Comer struggled with alcohol and depression.

Mr. Comer chose instead to live with his mother, Patricia Comer, who relayed to Ms. Sharp that he no longer drank, took medication for his mental health conditions and was desperate to spend time with his son.

“Are you OK if he sees Koah?” Ms. Sharp recalled Ms. Comer asking.

Ms. Sharp agreed to let Koah spend weekends with Mr. Comer and his mother.

In recent weeks, however, Mr. Comer’s texts to Ms. Sharp, who is 15 weeks pregnant with her second child with a different father, showed his growing jealousy and frustration over custody of Koah.

“U threatened it, u the one that wants to take him,” Ms. Sharp wrote to Mr. Comer weeks ago, referring to Koah, according to texts she shared with The New York Times. “I said what I mean. Plz stop texting me.”

“I don’t want to take him,” Mr. Comer said. “I want us to be a family.”

Then Mr. Comer sent a flurry of texts that Ms. Sharp did not reply to.

“I got toooo heated about the situation so I get not speaking to me anymore,” he wrote. “I want to be a family with real trust.”

After the most recent visit, Ms. Sharp waited for Mr. Comer and his mother to drop off Koah on Monday. They didn’t show. She asked Ms. Comer where Koah was. Ms. Comer thought he was home with his father, but she realized she was wrong when she got home.

Ms. Comer called 911 and told a dispatcher that her missing son, who was on probation, had “threatened to kill himself last night” and had asked “for some sleeping pills,” according to audio released by the county.

That morning, John Comer, who is separated from Ms. Comer, said he received an unexpected call from his son, who said he was in a disagreement with his mother and with Ms. Sharp over “how to take care of the baby.” He had Koah and needed a ride and a place to stay, so John Comer agreed to help.

In the car ride to John Comer’s house, which is hidden behind a dirt road and dense shrubbery, his son appeared stable, he said.

“I started quizzing him about the situation, if he had a working plan,” John Comer said. “He didn’t falter.”

Mr. Comer complained about his ex, accusing her of fostering an unsafe environment for their child. John Comer, who had rarely spoken to his son, was taking it all in as they arrived at his house. Koah began to cry, hungry and thirsty for milk. His diaper was dirty.

Mr. Comer changed him and fed him milk from a bottle.

Later that morning, after Mr. Comer’s father drove to work, he was left alone with Koah.

“I just figured he was wanting a place to stay, and they would work out something in the future,” John Comer said of Koah’s parents. “Everything seemed legit.”

Later that afternoon, John Comer received a call from the county sheriff. His son and grandson were missing. He also had missed calls from Ms. Comer.

Search parties fanned out across his property. Ms. Sharp, who suffers from a pregnancy complication characterized by extreme, persistent nausea, spoke with detectives and struggled to sleep that night through constant crying and vomiting.

Mr. Comer was found drunk by an old building on Monday night, his father said. A lead detective who spoke at Mr. Comer’s bond hearing on Thursday said he was unremorseful. John Comer, who spoke with investigators, said the authorities believed Koah would be somewhere near his property, given the brief timeline and surveillance footage that captured his son alone elsewhere later that day.

On Tuesday, John Comer said, a detective found a chunk of dirt that appeared to be disturbed. A dog sniffed it, and then crews rushed over with digging equipment. They heard muffled baby cries.

When Ms. Sharp was reunited with Koah at a hospital, she noticed scabs on his forehead that nurses initially thought were mud stains.

“I’m tired,” she said in the interview, adding: “But better now that I know he’s alive.”

Ms. Sharp paused. Koah sat quietly in another room, dazzled by Mickey Mouse twirling a magic wand on TV.

“Let me go check on him again,” she said.

Kirsten Noyes contributed research.

item.title: Unlike Other Countries, America’s Government Funds Its Air Infrastructure
item.description:
It took Canada two years to replace paper flight strips with electronic ones in air traffic control towers, a simple transition to avoid cascading delays. In the United States, the same project has taken more than four decades, and it is still not complete.

The example highlights an irony. Despite handling the most flights in the world, America’s air traffic control systems — still using 1980s-era equipment and prone to widespread failures — have lagged behind some global peers when it comes to improving technology.

A key difference, aviation experts say, is that the U.S. Federal Aviation Administration relies on Congress to fund crucial upgrades, while other countries have privatized their air traffic control. That has meant more money, more consistently, to invest in improving systems in places like Canada and the European Union, both considered success stories in aviation management.

The F.A.A.’s issuing of a nationwide ground stop on Friday underscored America’s aging infrastructure, which experts have warned for years is in urgent need of modernizing, and which critics say has been chronically underfunded. For decades, U.S. air traffic communications have relied on a system that runs on analog copper wire, floppy disks and alphabetical keyboards so old that the F.A.A. has difficulty sourcing spare parts.

Speaking to reporters after the outage, Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary, echoed those concerns, describing an air traffic control system stuck in the past, and demanding $50 billion from Congress to improve it.

“Canada and the European Union don’t have to worry about the public purse,” said John Gradek, an aviation management expert at McGill University. “They are masters of their own destiny.”

“The F.A.A. has been fighting this funding beast for decades and has to look for money at all times,” he added. “That is why they’re behind.”

America’s air traffic needs are complicated. The United States handles more flights and passengers than any other country, and does so over a large and complex geographic terrain. That means the advanced air traffic systems developed in Asia, like those of Korea, Malaysia or Singapore, are less useful as possible benchmarks than Canada or the European Union, Mr. Gradek said.

Canada became the first country in the world to privatize its air traffic control system, under a company called NAV Canada. Unlike the F.A.A., which relies on congressional appropriations, the company gets its money directly from airlines and airline customers. Many countries in Europe, including Germany and Switzerland, operate on hybrid public-private models that help finance a coordinated European Union traffic system. As in Canada, funding largely comes from users, not taxpayers.

This has allowed both Canada and the European Union to invest billions into updating systems without relying on lawmakers and to make headway on innovations like satellite-based tracking of flights. In Canada, the changes lowered prices for users and increased productivity, according to a July report by the Reason Foundation, a think tank.

A communications disruption set off by a copper-to-fiber upgrade at a remote site led to Friday’s shutdown, according to federal officials. Mr. Gradek pointed to that switch, which has proceeded in fits and starts for decades, as an example of how a difference in funding translates to a difference in how quickly things can get done.

America’s “25-year transition from copper wire to fiber is endemic to the type of organization that you have to fight for money every year to move this project one inch at a time,” he said.

Although the same upgrade is not entirely complete in Canada, according to NAV Canada, the majority of the work was finished in just 18 months, Mr. Gradek said.

item.title: Judge Blocks Immediate Closure of East Potomac Park for Trump Golf Project
item.description:
A federal judge on Saturday temporarily blocked the Trump administration from shuttering East Potomac Park in Washington, finding that the proposed closure appeared to be intended to start the process of transforming the area into a championship golf course.

President Trump had announced that the municipal golf course and park would close on Sunday, ahead of the renovation work that he had called for. The ruling by Judge Ana C. Reyes of the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia means the park will remain open for now.

In her 30-page order, Judge Reyes said that the Trump administration would not be responsible for operating the course while the case proceeds, but required the golf courses, paths and picnic areas in the park to remain “open and accessible to the public.”

Judge Reyes has for months been overseeing combative litigation over the future of the Washington park and golf course. A preservationist organization and local golfers sued in February, arguing that the project threatened to destroy a historic course that remained a cheap and accessible option for recreational players.

She had issued a series of rulings focused on a narrower dispute over whether the administration could clear out trees at the site. Saturday’s order was her first blocking work more generally at the park.

It came amid a larger standoff in which Judge Reyes has repeatedly accused administration officials of concealing their efforts to move forward with Mr. Trump’s ideas.

In her opinion, Judge Reyes left the Trump administration the option to shut down parts of the park that they deemed hazardous to the public, if they notified the court within 24 hours. But she found that most of the reasons the government had provided for shuttering the entire park on Sunday appeared “transparently pretextual.”

“The Department of the Interior has progressed from removing the trees to removing the people,” she wrote.

The order would require the park to stay open for two weeks.

During a hearing on Friday, Judge Reyes again peppered lawyers from the Justice Department with questions about the details of the plan, piecing together a sprawling record of the government’s involvement in an apparent effort to covertly speed Mr. Trump’s favored design forward.

Last week, she appointed a former U.S. attorney to serve as a so-called special master in the case investigating whether officials at the Justice and Interior Departments inappropriately withheld details from the court in October.

At the start of the five-hourhearing on Friday, she told lawyers she had seen reports of whistle-blowers claiming that some federal agencies had destroyed documents after the midterm elections.

She told the lawyers that if she came to learn that the Interior Department destroyed documents in defiance of her orders to preserve them, she would begin contempt-of-court proceedings in a “zeptosecond,” which she described as the shortest known unit of time.

As she had for weeks, she pressed government lawyers about whether agencies had started carrying out Mr. Trump’s plan for the peninsula, which would involve wiping out the public course, a picnic area at Hains Point, and running and cycling paths currently occupying the space.

Mr. Trump has promoted his plans for the course, but his lawyers have maintained for months that they are not set in stone, and that it would be premature for Judge Reyes to intervene.

Adam R.F. Gustafson, a government lawyer, said that despite the impending closure, renovation activity was not necessarily imminent.

He said there would be no immediate rush to build the course Mr. Trump had proposed, at least until the Interior Department had finished environmental reviews and other preparations.

“When the president speaks, the agency listens,” he said. “But the agency has to comply with law.”

Echoing arguments used in a lawsuit over the John F. Kennedy Center for Performing Arts, Mr. Gustafson said that years of neglect had left the course so dangerous that the government had been forced to announce the closure of the park to “protect life and limb.” He said that even though people were continuing to golf on the course as of Friday, safety concerns would mount after the course’s current operator, the National Links Trust, gave up its management of the property on Sunday. The National Links Trust agreed to relinquish control of the course after Mr. Trump made clear that he planned to close it.

Mr. Trump has repeatedly declared that the new course would be designed by Tom Fazio, a well-known architect who did work on other courses owned by the Trump Organization. Mr. Fazio’s involvement suggests that plans for the site are far from preliminary.

Judge Reyes on Friday asked Stanley Woodward Jr., a top Justice Department official, about Mr. Fazio’s role. Mr. Woodward responded that he would be “shocked to learn there is any contract with Fazio.”

“Closure does not make implementation of the Fazio plan any more likely,” Mr. Gustafson added, saying that Judge Reyes appeared to be “bootstrapping one decision to a future decision.”

Judge Reyes expressed skepticism, noting that the government had repeatedly claimed it was merely conducting routine maintenance work at the course even as it appeared to be advancing on the timeline for the overhaul that Mr. Trump had announced on social media.

“I spent 22 years at a law firm,” she said. “The most important thing I learned is that the most important thing a lawyer has is their credibility and their reputation.”

In her Saturday opinion, she concluded all the government’s justifications so far appeared to follow a longer-term effort to begin construction.

“President Trump directed this closure for one reason: so that work could begin on a new Fazio Design to replace the current East Potomac Golf Course,” she wrote.

item.title: What to Know About Continued Flight Disruptions
item.description:
Effects of a nationwide ground stop on air travel Friday evening, which stranded thousands of passengers and caused widespread delays, rippled into Saturday as airlines canceled thousands of flights and airports struggled to recover.

The air traffic control system, which faced a faulty upgrade that caused communications failures leading to the ground stop, is expected to be back to normal by Sunday night, said Bryan Bedford, who leads the Federal Aviation Administration. Flight schedules could take several days to return to normal.

Federal officials are still trying to determine who is at fault and have called for congressional funding to prevent similar failures. There is no evidence that the problem was caused by a cyberattack, officials have said.

Here’s what to know:

L3Harris, a contractor managing the F.A.A.’s telecoms network, made a standard upgrade at a remote air traffic location, federal officials said Saturday. L3Harris was conducting a routine task — replacing copper wire with more modern fiber optic cable — that was expected to pose no significant disruption to air traffic, said Sean Duffy, the transportation secretary.

But the switch from copper to fiber overwhelmed the system with levels of data it could not handle, prompting widespread communications failures across air traffic facilities that manage the national air space. Alarmed at the scope of the problems, officials issued a rare nationwide ground stop for hours.

Administration officials say it’s still unclear whether L3Harris or faulty equipment was to blame. L3Harris said in a statement on Saturday that it was supporting the F.A.A. investigation and that it “takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously.”

There was no evidence that nefarious activity, or the agency’s recent efforts to equip its air traffic control facilities with assistive A.I. technology, had played a role in triggering the issue, Mr. Duffy and Mr. Bedford said.

On Friday, Mr. Duffy faulted Congress for not providing adequate funding to overhaul the aging air traffic control system. On Friday, he asked for $50 billion to modernize the system, thrusting the funding issue to the forefront of the final days of G.O.P. control on Capitol Hill.

Last year, Congress approved $12.5 billion to help pay for upgrades to the air traffic communications system. Speaker Mike Johnson told Fox News on Saturday morning that he would seek to increase F.A.A. funding in an “aggressive legislative package” he planned to put forth before Democrats take control of both chambers.

Democrats said the Trump administration had more than enough money to allocate toward improvements, but that it had prioritized deportations over air safety. They vowed to hold the administration accountable for what had happened and said that Congress needed to begin investigating the administration’s failures.

For an aviation system to function well, availability of planes, crews and an open airport gate need to line up at the right time and place. It could take days for airlines to juggle their schedules, rebook passengers and reposition planes.

While airlines can try to make up for lost time after minor disruptions, bigger disruptions often require them to reset the network by canceling flights proactively.

On Friday, thousands of flights were halted. Many planes returned to the airports they had just taken off from, according to Cirium, an aviation data firm, crowding limited space on the ground while flight crews quickly hit their legal working limits.

Since individual airlines were not to blame for the upgrade that caused the ground stop, travelers can expect limited accommodations. In the United States, if your flight is canceled, significantly delayed or changed, airlines will try to rebook you on another flight. You’re also entitled to a refund as long as you choose to not take that flight.

Carriers including United Airlines, Delta Air Lines, JetBlue Airways, Alaska Airlines and Southwest Airlines have issued waivers allowing travelers to change or cancel their flights without incurring any change fees or fare differences.

Stranded travelers can consider other strategies to reach their destination, such as joining the standby list for an earlier flight or calling an airline’s international hotline, which will have fewer callers.

Karoun Demirjian, Annie Karni, Niraj Chokshi and Christine Chung contributed reporting.

item.title: Two Planes Collide on a Taxiway at Miami International Airport
item.description:
Two planes collided on a taxiway at Miami International Airport on Saturday night, officials said, a day after a nationwide ground stop disrupted air travel and stranded thousands of passengers.

The wingtip of a Copa Airlines Boeing 737 struck the nose of a UPS Boeing 767 around 9 p.m., according to the Federal Aviation Administration, which is investigating. Two people were treated at the scene for minor injuries, and flights were routed to other taxiways without disrupting airport operations, said Greg Chin, a spokesman for the Miami-Dade Aviation Department.

Air traffic controllers had told the UPS crew to give way to the Copa flight, the F.A.A. said. The Copa plane was taxiing to the gate, having arrived from Panama City, while the UPS plane was taxiing for departure to Bogotá, Colombia. The planes made contact at the intersection of two taxiways, Mr. Chin said.

The collision came just over two months after an Amazon cargo jet overran a runway at the same airport, striking two vehicles and killing five people. An air-traffic controller had failed to warn the pilots about windy conditions when giving them permission to land, according to a federal report.

The incident also came amid widespread disruption to air travel after a rare nationwide ground stop on Friday. Thousands of flights were canceled on Saturday as airlines worked to reposition aircraft and crews. Federal officials said an upgrade to air traffic control telecommunications equipment triggered communications failures that prompted Friday’s halt.

item.title: ‘I Love Being a Girl’: Inside the Life of a Sorority Influencer
item.description:
The Alpha Phi sorority house at the University of Arizona occupies a professionally decorated Spanish colonial-style mansion just off campus. There’s a chandeliered dining room, two pink-and-baby-blue living rooms and a tanning area on the roof.

It’s where Haley DeKreek, a 20-year-old junior, lives with her closest friends. It’s also the backdrop to her budding career. Her work takes place mostly in her room, but she picks up the rewards in the mailroom just off the foyer.

Perpetually suffused with floral perfume, it overflows with packages, many of them hers: boxes with dresses for formals or matching yoga sets, boxes of makeup, hair products and skin care. Some she ordered herself, but many are freebies from brands that have spotted her potential as a TikTok influencer, a one-girl campus marketing powerhouse. Nearly all are destined to appear in the many-stepped “get ready with me” videos she has posted since she was a first-year student rushing sororities.

With more than 45,000 TikTok followers, a gift for self-deprecating humor, a talent manager in Los Angeles and several paid brand deals (the biggest worth $3,000), Ms. DeKreek says she can now pay for all her own shopping, food, vacations and beauty services, just by doing what she has loved since kindergarten, when she played with her mom’s makeup and recorded videos making slime.

She never attends class — not in person, anyway. Her major, retail and consumer science, is entirely online. Apt, given her chosen career path: influencing.

Football players aren’t the only college students who have learned to sell their images for profit. The boom in sorority TikTok videos known as #Rushtok has proved, especially to marketers, that sorority sisters can command audiences all over America.

Ms. DeKreek’s sorority “big,” or mentor, has nearly 800,000 TikTok followers and a Porsche. Sisters at several sororities on Greek Row serve as brand ambassadors, posting about free products and hosting events like yoga on the lawn with the active wear company Alo. On Alpha Phi’s Instagram, the well-known fashion influencers Brigette and Danielle Pheloung visit to promote a “lower sugar” snack, and sorority sisters model brand-sponsored merchandise in posts accompanied by discount codes.

In a recent survey, nearly four in 10 Gen Z respondents said they would take a million social media followers over a steady 9-to-5 job. At several universities, including at the rival Arizona State University, students can now major in content creation.

For Ms. DeKreek, college coursework appears strictly secondary to the business of being @HaleyDeKreek.

In the days before Arizona’s homecoming football game against Iowa State in October, when fraternities and sororities threw events almost every night, I followed her as she drove around Tucson in her cobalt-blue Jeep with oversized wheels, going from beauty appointment to beauty appointment to prepare for the week’s events.

Not that it feels like work. “I love being a girl,” Ms. DeKreek said.

For all that, Ms. DeKreek is ambivalent about social media and the Botox-and-fillers culture she sees on campus — even as her appearance testifies to its pressures, even as she sells products for upholding it.

“People come here and they’re instantly intimidated by the pretty girls,” she said. “They’ll see these videos online, they’ll see the people around them, and instantly start judging themselves.”

She added: “Being a woman in this society is just, like, so overwhelming even compared to five to 10 years ago.”

Wednesday, 1 p.m.: Eyelash lift and tint

Americans have spent the last year agog at male looksmaxxers, who take hammers to their own jaws and inject themselves with dubious substances in the name of beauty. But women have been practicing time-consuming, expensive, invasive and potentially self-destructive interventions for a long, long time. And they’re starting younger than ever.

Twenty-somethings get preventive Botox. Teenagers get fillers. Preteens crowd the aisles of Sephora, purchasing anti-aging serums in bottles the colors of Nerds candy. In a 2025 survey of American plastic surgeons, 57 percent reported that more patients under 30 were requesting cosmetic procedures or injectables. Older women seek to look like young women, and younger women chase the perfected visions of themselves they can generate on their phones.

At 20, Ms. DeKreek said, she has already had lip filler and breast reduction surgery (her large chest made everyday activities physically painful). There have also been multiple rounds of Botox in her forehead (to keep her eyebrows level), cheeks (to stop nighttime jaw-clenching), armpits (to stop sweating) and upper lip (a “lip flip” that bestows a fuller look).

She has a hairstylist for her extensions and a friend who gives her regular spray tans. At home in Folsom, Calif., an affluent Sacramento suburb, she has a therapist and a go-to aesthetician. Today, a Tucson aesthetician gives her an eyebrow-smoothing treatment, and then perma-curls and dyes her lashes in a procedure called a lift and tint.

Ms. DeKreek’s parents sanctioned her procedures, except one injection she got in high school, said her mother, Sandy DeKreek. Then, she thought Haley was too young. Now, proud of her daughter, she says Haley is mature enough to decide.

You hardly have to be an influencer to want to polish your appearance, even if at great effort and cost; being a young woman tends to suffice. For an influencer like Ms. DeKreek, however, beauty draws attention, generating more motivation to be beautiful, encouraging more procedures, which, when posted online, yield money to pay for yet more beauty.

Wednesday, 5 p.m.: Spray tan

Thursday, 8 a.m.: Morning skin care

Ms. DeKreek starts every day by applying six of the many skin care products stored in the white minifridge on her vanity — the first half of her routine.

Thursday, 8:30 a.m.: Wellness walk

Wearing patches to brighten the barely-voting-age skin under their eyes, she and her friend Lea Gorham set off for their morning “wellness walk.”

Ms. DeKreek and her friends gild their days with healthfulness, adopting trends infused with Make America Healthy Again buzzwords. Seed oils and processed foods are out; journaling, early-morning Pilates, protein, probiotics and gut health supplements are in.

As they power-walk through campus, Ms. Gorham debates whether to get lip filler or just a cheaper lip flip. She doesn’t like the way she smiles.

“I don’t necessarily need it, but it’s like, everyone else at this school has it,” she said.

Both procedures are available at a local med spa, where until a couple years ago, undergraduates could use Cat Cash — student bursary funds, generally replenished by parents — to pay for fillers by swiping their student IDs. The spa takes Cat Cash only for non-injectable beauty services now, but lips keep getting flipped.

Thursday, 9:45 a.m.: Morning routine, part 2

Ms. DeKreek begins the second half of her skin care regimen, running a pink electric device over her face, draining her lymph nodes, depuffing invisible puffiness.

To her, beauty helps her feel like her “best self.” Makeup, she said, is like an “art form.”

The most creative and artistic of the four DeKreek sisters, according to her family, Haley began filming videos of herself as a child of 6 or 7, pretending to cook for an audience. She started getting hair highlights in fifth grade. In middle school, she styled her hair for cheerleading competitions and watched hours of YouTube makeup tutorials. In high school, she worked at a hair salon, earning a discount on hair extensions, and taught herself video editing so she could film school football games and other events for student government.

Before rushing sororities, she watched videos for outfit inspiration and tips. With an older sister’s encouragement, she started posting her own rush outfits and makeup routines.

But she’s keenly conscious of social media’s effect on others’ self-esteem. Pushing back in her own small way, she is open about her stubborn acne. She has posted her beauty procedures, not wanting to present her appearance as natural. Having struggled with anxiety and the adjustment to Arizona’s hard-charging party scene her first year of college, she says she wants to post more about mental health.

Thursday, 12 p.m.: Blowout

As Ms. DeKreek fluffs her freshly blow-dried extensions, her hairstylist sets up a tripod to document the final touches. Ms. DeKreek shoots her own videos in the mirror. “You want to post and I’ll repost?” she asks David Gonzalez, her stylist.

Thursday, 1 p.m.: Quick shopping stop

Thursday, 4 p.m.: Getting ready

It’s Ms. DeKreek’s favorite part of the day: getting ready. Tonight is “Greek wedding,” an annual tradition in which sororities and fraternities stage mock weddings between seniors, complete with funny speeches and parties.

Ms. DeKreek has never had a boyfriend. Though she eventually wants a family, she describes college hookup culture and setup dates as “a waste of time.”

“I just want to focus on myself,” she said, “and the right one will come along at some point.”

It’s a common sentiment among young women, who research indicates are having fewer romantic relationships than past generations.

Nearly three hours after starting to get ready, she heads to Ms. Gorham’s room to finish. It’s crowded with girls in long black dresses and small designer purses, smoothing, spraying, adjusting, asking to borrow one another’s heels.

“Cute!” they compliment one another. “Cute, cute, cute!”

Friday, 1 p.m.: Monthly facial

Saturday, 10 a.m.: Getting ready for Game Day

After an hour of curling her hair, Ms. DeKreek and her roommate deftly paint, blend, dab, brush, spray and dry their faces. Taylor Swift, Beyoncé and Christina Aguilera sing from a speaker. Friends burst in without knocking to rummage through their wardrobes, needing to borrow cutoffs or jewelry.

This is what she means when she says, tenderly, “It’s like girlhood, all of us together.” She loves getting ready so much, she says, she sometimes doesn’t even feel like going out after.

Thinking about how others see her, after all, is “just kind of a dead end,” she said. “I’ve only found fulfillment through taking care of myself.”

If it seems paradoxical to find inner fulfillment through outer enhancement, well, that’s the promise society has held out to women since long before she was born.

She slides on a strapless gingham-and-lace minidress. The others are ready, all of them clomping around in tan knee-high boots, but she’s still dabbing and brushing. She unpins her curls, releasing bombshell cascades. Golden bangles click over her wrists. Before the mirror, she turns this way and that, all alone as a din of voices rises outside the door.

item.title: Woman Who Reported Assault Accuses University of Violating Consumer Law
item.description:
A former student who was sexually assaulted at Texas Christian University is suing the school using an unusual legal strategy, claiming it violated a consumer protection law in another state.

Sexual assault lawsuits against universities are difficult to win, often requiring proof that the universities acted with “deliberate indifference,” according to KC Johnson, a Brooklyn College professor who has studied lawsuits filed under Title IX of the Civil Rights Act.

As a result, plaintiffs have tried workarounds over the years. Even so, Dr. Johnson described a consumer protection claim as “highly unusual,” if not novel.

The lawsuit says T.C.U., a private university in Fort Worth, Texas, violated the Virginia Consumer Protection Act by misleading the woman, a Virginia resident, about the safety of its campus.

If successful, the lawsuit, brought by a woman identified only as Jane Doe, could broaden legal avenues for students frustrated with the outcomes of their complaints.

T.C.U. has argued that it does supply “services” in Virginia and that the woman wouldn’t have a complaint against T.C.U. if she had not attended school in Texas, asking that the case be dismissed or transferred to Texas.

Rulings on those questions are pending in a Virginia federal court.

In a statement, the university said it strongly disputed the lawsuit’s allegations and said the Virginia Consumer Protection Act claim “lacks legal and factual merit.”

The lawsuit claims the university’s recruiting practices are deceptive, but in its statement, T.C.U. said that information on campus crime statistics, including sex crimes, is made public and is available to prospective students.

The complainant has a powerful ally in Jay Jones, the Virginia attorney general, whose office wants the court to consider his brief in the case, arguing that the Virginia Consumer Protection Act, adopted to protect the state’s residents from fraudulent vendors, applies to out-of-state entities.

The attorney general’s office wrote that the law is clear: “Its prohibitions and protections extend beyond the borders of the commonwealth.”

The young woman at the center of the case attended high school in Virginia and, according to her lawsuit, was attracted to T.C.U. by a scholarship as well as the university’s representation that its campus was a safe place for women, the lawsuit said.

Her lawsuit said that she and her male assailant were at a party in fall 2024, her freshman year, where they both had alcoholic drinks.

After sharing an Uber back to the dorm where they both lived, the two made out in Ms. Doe’s bed for about 30 minutes until the male student left to go to the bathroom.

The woman fell asleep. She woke up to find the male student having sexual intercourse with her without a condom, the lawsuit said. It was an outcome she says she had neither consented to nor wanted, according to the lawsuit. She ordered him to leave.

The next day, the woman asked the student to meet and surreptitiously recorded him with her phone. In the recording, he admitted he had penetrated her without first seeking verbal consent, the documents said.

Following a hearing, a university panel concluded that the young man was guilty of sexual assault because he had sexual intercourse without consent.

The panel placed him on probation, ordered him to change dorms, required him to watch video trainings about “mutual consent,” and to write a paper of reflection.

Unsatisfied with his punishment, the woman submitted an appeal to the panel.

“The term nonconsensual sexual intercourse sounds so benign. But let’s call it what it is. In almost every state in America, nonconsensual sexual intercourse is rape,” she wrote.

“And what is the punishment for rape at T.C.U., according to the panel members? The punishment is homework!”

Following her appeal, the panel did not change its punishment.

After Ms. Doe’s lawyer sent T.C.U. a letter laying out what he viewed as its failures in the case, the university’s leadership overturned the panel’s decision, calling it inappropriate, and ordered the student suspended for two semesters.

By that time, the school year had ended and the young woman had left the T.C.U. campus for good.

The male student was not identified in the documents and could not be reached for comment.

The lawsuit argues that T.C.U.’s policies encourage rape. “Male students at T.C.U. know that nothing will happen to them for raping T.C.U.’s female students,” it said.

Shiwali Patel, senior director of education justice for the National Women’s Law Center, said that, like Jane Doe, many women had been unhappy with how universities responded to their complaints, noting that the Trump administration had weakened regulations governing Title IX.

“I think its important to hold educational institutions accountable for what their promises are to students and their families when students are choosing to attend,” she said. “It wasn’t the safe place she assumed it would be.”

Ms. Doe’s lawyer, Thomas M. Wolf, argues the case is simple, saying, “Why would they be treated any differently from another vendor who misleads a Virginia consumer?”
