item.title: The Reward for Black Women’s Work in Georgia: Leaders Who Look Like Them
item.description:
Mary-Pat Hector volunteered on Election Day to help get dozens of voters to the polls in Georgia, and she had spent months doing everything she could to energize other young people to support Democratic candidates. She was a Gen Z torchbearer for traditions of organizing and mobilizing handed down over generations of Black women. And she was prepared for a good night.

She was hopeful that Keisha Lance Bottoms would win, making Georgia the first state to elect a Black woman as governor. But then history kept being made: Up and down the ballot, Black women, all Democrats, claimed positions that had long been occupied by Republican men.

She called her mentor, a veteran organizer in the state. Both women were stunned. A future that they thought might be attainable some day in Georgia was suddenly materializing.

“We both just cried on the phone,” Ms. Hector, 28, said, “because we have been doing this work for so long.” Finally, she added, they could “see the fruits of our labor.”

For decades, Black women have been a trusted base of support for the Democratic Party in Georgia and also its most relied-upon foot soldiers. They have knocked on doors, registered friends and neighbors to vote, driven strangers to the polls and coaxed people who had all but written off the government to show up anyway. It was the incremental, sometimes inspiring, often frustrating work that revived the fortunes of Democrats in Georgia after years of Republican control.

For the first time, the result of their efforts was more than a win for their party. Their reward was a mirror: The governor, the attorney general, the secretary of state and the insurance commissioner will all be Black women. Only one of the top eight state elected offices will not be held by a Black woman, and he is still a Democrat. The speaker of the House is also likely to be the first Black woman in the position, as Democrats gained a majority for the first time in more than 20 years.

“I don’t know where in the world you have eight Black women in charge of a government,” said Penny Brown Reynolds, who was elected secretary of state. “It’s a seat at the table. It’s having the authority to make the decisions.”

Throughout her career, she had often been the first and only Black woman in a role. Now, she said, “I’m not walking into the room alone.”

On the campaign trail as candidates, they did not lead with their identity. Frustrations with inflation, health care costs and voting rights dominated stump speeches. And some Black women casting ballots in Georgia said that they had not made their choices based primarily on the candidates’ identities.

“I did my research on all the candidates, and I liked how each of them stood on issues,” said Bernadette Scruggs, a 79-year-old retired Chicago public-school teacher and longtime Democrat who moved to Grovetown, Ga., near Augusta. “Their values were similar to mine.”

But even so, the weight of these wins was not lost on her or others. There was sweet satisfaction in seeing women who are descendants of enslaved people, whose ancestors lived through segregation and whose right to vote came from bloodshed and sacrifice take the helm of a state that had once been in the Confederacy.

It also felt like something of a salve after the sting of setbacks in recent election cycles, in which Black women lost in statewide races even as other Democrats succeeded.

“We have been tilling the land for a long time,” said Sherrell Byrd, co-founder and executive director of Sowega Rising, a nonpartisan organization supporting voter engagement in southwestern Georgia. “We have had some seasons where we didn’t get a harvest, but we kept at it, we kept fertilizing.”

The election turned out to be a transformative one far beyond Georgia. Democrats notched surprising wins in places like Mississippi, South Carolina and Texas, long considered Republican strongholds.

But in Georgia, organizers and activists believe that years of diligent work paired with the lessons of past disappointments allowed Democrats to capitalize on voters’ frustration with President Trump and their desire to punish incumbents.

The historic sweep in Georgia was more than a decade in the making, going back to Stacey Abrams, the first Black woman in the country to win a major party nomination for governor.

She lost her campaigns in 2018 and 2022 but was credited with building the infrastructure to harness the demographic shifts that had come with Georgia’s explosive growth.

That progress helped pave the way for Democratic victories in the 2020 election cycle; Joseph R. Biden Jr. became the first Democratic nominee to win Georgia in a presidential election in nearly three decades, and Jon Ossoff and Raphael Warnock ousted the state’s Republican incumbent senators.

Ms. Abrams’s campaigns also helped in “normalizing Black women in elected office and normalizing Black women being at the top of the ticket,” said Glynda C. Carr, the president and chief executive of Higher Heights for America, a political action committee that supports Black women running for office across the country.

Still, Ms. Bottoms and others were running in a climate that had shifted considerably even in a few years. The country had emerged from the pandemic, and the reckoning over racism prompted by the murder of George Floyd, a Black man killed by a white police officer in Minneapolis, had given way to backlash.

Ms. Bottoms would often share her family’s history, tracing it to the tiny town of Crawfordville and her great-great-grandfather, who was enslaved. But she typically would do so only after bringing up the burdens of a higher cost of living that she blamed on Mr. Trump.

“I was never running because I was a Black woman,” Ms. Bottoms said on “The Interview,” a New York Times show. “I wake up as a Black woman every day, so I didn’t feel the need to lead with that. It speaks for itself.”

Ms. Brown Reynolds, who will oversee elections, campaigned on strengthening voting rights and protecting access to the polls. She also highlighted her varied experience — serving as a civil rights lawyer in the Biden administration and working for the state’s attorney general’s office.

“Generations of Black women have built institutions,” she said. “We’ve educated our children. We’ve run organizations. We’ve done the work without being afforded the authority.”

Ms. Hector, the Gen Z organizer, said that the candidates’ identity mattered in the sense that their practical and lived experience gave them credibility with voters who were exasperated with elected officials they believe had lost sight of their most urgent problems.

“They just want candidates who get it,” said Ms. Hector, the executive director of Rise, an organization mobilizing college-age voters. “They recognized that those were the people that were going to get it done.”

Mary Blakely has been stopping people outside grocery stores and churches and in parks around Albany, Ga., most every election season for more than two decades, offering the same simple civics lesson. “You have to vote to change things,” Ms. Blakely, 78, said.

This election brought the changes she had hoped for: to see more people who looked like her leading a state where they have a history of being overlooked and mistreated. “Well, this just feels great,” Ms. Blakely said, savoring Ms. Bottoms’s win most of all. “The first Black governor. Female. I am proud of that.”

The jubilation immediately after the election has been followed by a more sobering realization for the foot soldiers: They had won a battle. But they still had to keep marching.

For one thing, some said, there was a responsibility to create a sustainable new reality, one that would endure not only in Georgia but across the South. This year’s wins could not be a blip, they said.

“We’ve got to make sure that we’re not just the first to do something,” said Tanya Miller, who was elected attorney general, “but we create a pathway for others to follow behind.”

One lesson of the midterms had been that voters were fickle and political fortunes could change rapidly, and these new leaders could easily inherit the anger now directed at Republicans. And the perennial lesson of Southern history is that Black political and social gains are often followed by backlash.

Ms. Hector said the work now was to protect against that. That would mean urging patience from voters, as the solutions they crave will most likely not come immediately or without compromise. She also wants to make sure the incoming elected officials are held accountable and scrutinized on their ability to deliver, but without being held to an unfair standard.

“We can’t expect them to just snap their fingers and make things work out,” she said. She added, “I don’t want people to also feel like because we’ve had this win, this win it’s enough.”

item.title: Embattled Federal Employees Look to a Democratic Congress for a Lifeline
item.description:
Since the start of his second term, President Trump has gone after the federal work force, shearing 17 percent of employees, stripping away centuries of experience in medicine, law and science, and politicizing jobs meant to be nonpartisan.

Embattled current and former workers are now looking to Democrats, newly empowered after the Republican rout in the midterm elections, for help.

But the sweeping Democratic victories came with competing ideas for change, starting with issues like affordability, health care and the war in Iran. That could mean that any reversal of Mr. Trump’s cuts may have to wait.

Then there is the reality that a Democratic-led Congress is only going to be able to do so much while Mr. Trump is still in the White House.

“We’re playing a long game here while we’re trying to prevent and undo as much damage as possible in the short term,” said Representative James Walkinshaw, a Democrat from a Northern Virginia district that is home to many current and former federal workers. Mr. Walkinshaw, who helped create the Congressional Federal Workforce Caucus earlier this year, said he expected the Trump administration to continue its attacks on the federal work force.

“But now we have some constitutional and legal authority to push back,” he said.

Current and former federal workers have been waiting 20 months for this moment. More than 389,000 employees left the government last year, a mix of people who were fired or pressured to leave, according to government data. The Agriculture, Health and Human Services, Interior and Treasury Departments suffered some of the biggest hits.

The White House has defended Mr. Trump’s cuts, and has said that the government is leaner and more efficient, an argument that former and current workers dispute. They point to widespread chaos and vacancies that have left basic work, such as getting grants out the door, delayed.

Their wish list for the incoming Congress is long.

Some want Congress to reconstitute the U.S. Agency for International Development and improve how it handles humanitarian and foreign assistance. They want their collective bargaining rights returned. They also want help burnishing the reputation of the federal work force after the Trump administration cast it as full of do-nothing bureaucrats.

Some current and former federal workers most want accountability, including congressional hearings that would force Trump administration officials to explain why they rescinded funds allocated by Congress, conducted widespread layoffs, and canceled contracts and grants.

“A lot of this will take a long time,” said Aryn Melton Backus, a co-founder of the National Public Health Coalition, a nonprofit group composed of fired and laid off members of the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention. She spoke in her personal capacity and not for the C.D.C., as she is still on paid administrative leave.

Ms. Melton Backus said that a Democratic majority in Congress still offered more hope to whistle-blowers, because lawmakers could hold hearings and call witnesses.

“Part of the attitude over the past year and a half,” she said, “is people have been like, ‘Well, if I do blow the whistle, nothing’s going to happen. So then, I’m risking my career for, you know, something potentially not happening.’”

Across the federal diaspora, there is a sense of guarded optimism.

“They feel like there is a real hope, you know, because these last 20 months have been very devastating for them,” said Everett Kelley, the national president of the American Federation of Government Employees, the largest labor union for federal workers. “Just the mere fact that they feel like somebody that is going to at least stand up to the corruption, stand up to the bullying, and, you know, the dismantling of the government. They feel good about that.”

Agan Smalley, the president of Local 777 of the International Federation of Professional and Technical Engineers and a geologist in the Army Corps of Engineers, said she was looking forward to her union’s annual legislative conference in Washington in February, after two years of being ignored by many Republicans. The conference provides opportunities for workers to speak directly with lawmakers and their staff members about policies and workers’ rights.

“Some of the way things are supposed to be done will be happening again,” she said.

Sarah Kobrin, an employee at the National Institutes of Health, said that she was happy with the midterm elections results, but that the deep cuts to medical research and grant funding had been so vast that it would take much more than federal dollars to recoup the losses.

“It was a big battle to win. But it is far from winning the war,” she said, speaking in her personal capacity and not for the agency. Part of winning the war, she said, was limiting the authority Mr. Trump had given to Russell T. Vought, the director of the Office of Management and Budget and the architect of the most consequential measures to dismantle the federal government.

The breadth of repairs to the government that will be needed is clear to Zach Dembo, a first-time Democratic candidate who flipped a House district in Kentucky that had been held by a Republican since 2013. Mr. Dembo, who served in the Navy and left his job as a federal prosecutor in 2025, is among several incoming lawmakers who are former federal workers.

Mr. Dembo said he saw the administration’s efforts to politicize the government as a part of the corruption that many voters had complained of during his campaign.

“We’re all committed to a federal government that operates free of politicization,” Mr. Dembo said. “I think a lot of us never would have ran. We wanted to stay being feds if it weren’t for all the nonsense going on.”

item.title: After Midterms Triumph, Democrats Look Quickly and Eagerly Ahead to 2028
item.description:
Even as Democrats across the country continue to revel in their sweeping midterm election victories, politicians, donors and campaign strategists have quickly begun looking ahead to what is widely expected to be a crowded and contentious 2028 presidential campaign.

Would-be Democratic presidential candidates have spread across the globe over the past week, headlining events aimed at lifting their national profiles, appearing with foreign leaders, schmoozing donors and scouting for political talent at happy hours with ambitious campaign operatives.

In Denver, at least eight potential candidates gathered for a three-day conference aptly titled “What’s Next.” Along the California coast, Senator Mark Kelly of Arizona led journalists and social media influencers on a tour of the aircraft carrier he served on as a U.S. Navy pilot. And Gov. Gavin Newsom of California appeared at a United Nations climate summit in Turkey, where he told Turkish news media that he planned to decide in late January if he would run for president in 2028 — the most specific timeline he has offered yet.

While no one has formally entered the presidential race, the passing of the midterm elections has given Democrats license to include themselves in increasingly public discussions about who is going to run and what they would bring to a contest that could include more than two dozen candidates.

“We have got to have an ideological conversation within our family, within our party,” Gov. Josh Shapiro of Pennsylvania said in an interview. “Whatever comes in the future, I’m going to be a part of that.”

The conference in Denver, a lavish gathering in the city’s River North Art District, amounted to an opening salvo from centrists to influence the direction of their party, as Democrats continued to chart their path out of the political wilderness and, they hoped, into the White House. The event was part candidate cattle call and part speed dating for potential campaign staff.

There were framed Art Deco-style posters on the walls for the event’s featured speakers — one was just the word “Raimondo” six times in lowercase blue and purple font, referring to Gina Raimondo, the former commerce secretary. Some attendees wore hats that read “Tax and Spend Liberal.”

In the final hours, the conference was upended by a nationwide ground stop that disrupted the travel plans of some of the biggest rising stars in the party. But between drinking cocktails and rebooking flights, the jockeying for the party’s future direction was in full force.

High-wattage midterm winners like Senator-elect James Talarico of Texas and Governor-elect Rob Sand of Iowa took victory laps and urged fellow Democrats to follow their leads. Lesser-known members of Congress with high ambitions spoke about their hopes of building their own national profiles.

Just about everybody talked about who might run for president.

“There’s a lot of people who have basically been running for the past two years, right?” Senator Elissa Slotkin of Michigan said in an interview. “We should accept a big primary. I think that we should not try to whittle it down.”

Ms. Slotkin said she would decide by early 2027 whether to run herself.

Senator Cory Booker of New Jersey, who ran for president in 2020, said in an interview that he was weighing another campaign because he wanted to try to be an uplifting and healing figure in a country that had so often found itself divided.

“There’s a realignment that’s happening that undermines what our algorithms tell us and what the 24-hour networks tell us,” said Mr. Booker, who coasted to re-election this month. “I’m going to use this platform I have for at least the next six years to talk about ending the false divides and bringing us together to what I think is a great common purpose as a country.”

And Senator Raphael Warnock of Georgia, who is senior pastor of the Ebenezer Baptist Church in Atlanta, described the kind of candidate that he believed that the party needed, with a profile that sounded remarkably like his own.

“We suffer not from a poverty of resources, but a moral imagination,” Mr. Warnock said in an interview. “I think the American people want someone in this moment who will help us all to believe that we can do big things in this country.”

Even those who had not been on the national radar, like Representative Joe Neguse of Colorado, urged reporters not to count them out for a presidential run.

“Insofar as one has a microphone and is willing to share with your colleagues and the country those new ideas, I suspect that there will be an audience to hear it,” Mr. Neguse said in an interview.

Mr. Newsom, in an interview before his overseas trip, warned against the impulse to translate the party’s sweeping successes last week to an election two years from now.

“We tend to wildly over-read midterm elections in this country,” he said.

Yet there were plenty of jubilant Democrats happily anticipating that their 2026 victories would lead to 2028 triumphs. Mr. Talarico, in a speech at the Denver convention on Thursday, told the audience, “We are within striking distance of a supermajority, and a supermajority requires a super agenda.”

Still others wanted to force a more divisive conversation about who should be Senate majority leader. Senator Chris Van Hollen of Maryland drew a large crowd on Friday morning as he made his pitch to oust Senator Chuck Schumer of New York.

“Voters fired Trump and his policies of corruption, the war and high costs, but they haven’t fully hired the Democrats,” Mr. Van Hollen said in an interview. “We need to earn the voters’ trust, and to do that we need to end business as usual, attack the status quo and elect new leadership.”

The Denver gathering was hosted by a new group called Majority Democrats, which hails from the party’s moderate wing and is focused on fostering a new generation of leaders. Its biggest donors include Stephen and Sue Mandel, hedge fund billionaires; the former New York City Mayor Michael R. Bloomberg; and James and Kathryn Murdoch.

The vibes were nearly euphoric at the happy hours and parties, including one for Democrats from the first six states on the Democratic Party’s 2028 primary calendar. Senior aides to would-be presidential candidates mingled with the sort of people whose endorsements would soon be sought after.

Don Scott, the speaker of the Virginia House of Delegates, said he had already heard from seven prospective Democratic presidential candidates. Ms. Slotkin said at least a dozen potential candidates had called her to talk about Michigan.

“If you want to be president, you gotta come to the mother of presidents,” Mr. Scott said. “They’re going to have to touch some of that dirt in Virginia.”

Some top contenders, like Gov. JB Pritzker of Illinois and Gov. Wes Moore of Maryland, did not attend the Denver event but sent top aides.

Mr. Kelly skipped the conference to highlight his career as a Navy pilot and NASA astronaut. After visiting his former aircraft carrier in San Diego, Mr. Kelly went to Los Angeles to visit his former space shuttle, the Endeavour, which is now on display at a new exhibit.

“I just don’t have a typical background,” Mr. Kelly said in an interview, acknowledging that it could be both a detriment and an asset if he decided to run for president.

David Axelrod, who directed Barack Obama’s presidential campaigns and has since become one of the party’s wise men, noted the unpredictability of the coming campaign.

“This is the first election I can remember where the field is wide open and there’s no front-runner,” he said. “We have a whole new cast of characters.”

item.title: Lutnick Pushed to Weaken Chip Rules That Overlap With His Family Business
item.description:
In Malaysia’s lush southern peninsula, a data center known as A201 is set to open next year, packed with hundreds of millions of dollars in Nvidia’s most advanced artificial intelligence servers.

The data center plans to supply this computing power to a Chinese tech giant. The setup is legal and profitable. It will also sidestep U.S. rules that ban sales of the most advanced A.I. chips directly to Chinese firms.

The company operating the data center is a client of Cantor Fitzgerald, the financial services firm formerly led by Howard Lutnick, the commerce secretary, who handed off leadership of it to his sons. Mr. Lutnick is now writing the rules that would have a substantial effect on the data center’s business.

Mr. Lutnick has been seen as a force slowing rules that would clamp down on the sale of Nvidia chips to data centers like A201, which sit outside China but provide A.I. computing power to Chinese firms.

The Trump administration, concerned about ceding the country’s advantage in A.I., bans the sale of cutting-edge chips to China. But it has been embroiled in an internal debate for much of the past two years over how far to go in limiting chip sales to data centers in Southeast Asia. On one side of the debate are China hawks, who see the data centers as a way for Beijing to do an end run around the chip sales ban. On the other are officials, most prominently Mr. Lutnick, who are pushing against going too far in limiting the ability of U.S. companies like Nvidia to sell their products in Asia.

Recently, Mr. Lutnick has been advocating a less stringent version of those controls under consideration, which could cut back on Nvidia’s business by giving the U.S. government more oversight of chip sales to international data centers. It is the latest example of Mr. Lutnick’s soft touch on chip regulation, which has prompted criticism from lawmakers and others in the administration.

Cantor Fitzgerald has had business dealings with several data center companies in Southeast Asia that cater to Chinese clients, and could be affected by the regulations Mr. Lutnick is drafting, a review by The New York Times has found.

Cantor Fitzgerald served as a designated sales agent for an equity offering of up to $1 billion this year by Bitdeer, the Singaporean firm that will operate data center A201, in addition to having other financial ties to various global data center businesses. The relationship between the two companies began as early as 2024, when Cantor Fitzgerald helped Bitdeer arrange a stock offering of up to $250 million.

Mr. Lutnick steered Cantor Fitzgerald for decades, before recusing himself when he joined the Trump administration last year. The Commerce Department says Mr. Lutnick has complied with all ethics agreements, and his former business is now run by his sons.

These dealings are just a tiny portion of Cantor’s business, which stretches from investment banking and trading to real estate. Other investment banks have similar partnerships, and there is no evidence that Cantor’s investments influenced Mr. Lutnick’s deliberations.

But the overlapping relationships are the latest indication of the potential conflicts that exist given Mr. Lutnick’s role in shaping rules around U.S. technology exports. And they demonstrate how the U.S. ban on selling chips directly to China has led to an explosion of data centers in Southeast Asia aimed at Chinese customers. It is now up to Mr. Lutnick to decide whether to tighten the rules in ways that would cut off this avenue.

In the administration, Mr. Lutnick has been seen as one of Nvidia’s strongest champions.

His department has been increasingly criticized in recent months for giving Nvidia unusual access to rule-making and investigations, and standing in the way of sanctions on Nvidia’s customers.

The issue has been thrust into the spotlight in recent weeks with the scandal over the Nvidia chief executive Jensen Huang’s affair with a woman the U.S. government deemed to be a Chinese intelligence asset.

The woman, Alice Huang, had led Megaspeed, a firm that set up data centers in Southeast Asia to serve Chinese companies. The U.S. government is also investigating Megaspeed for illegally smuggling chips into China.

The United States in late 2022 started banning exports of Nvidia’s advanced chips directly to China, out of concern the chips could help Beijing crack American encryption and design new weapons.

But while Chinese firms cannot buy Nvidia’s most advanced chips outright, nothing stops them from renting those chips in data centers in Malaysia, Indonesia or Thailand.

The arrangement is viewed by many in Washington as a harmful loophole. While some argue that the sales help U.S. leadership in technology, many in the administration have argued for clamping down, and Congress is considering a bipartisan bill to do so.

In its final weeks, the Biden administration issued global rules to restrict the ability of Chinese companies to remotely access U.S. chips. But President Trump revoked those rules when he came into office, arguing that they stifled American business and innovation.

Trump officials said they would introduce a new rule to replace the Biden ones. But they have struggled to reconcile competing views in the administration about how aggressive the rules should be.

Mr. Lutnick has been described as delaying or deferring these technology controls at several points in the past year, arguing that they could affect companies like Nvidia, or U.S. trade relations with China and other countries.

People familiar with the discussions say the Commerce Department has pushed for a more scaled-back version of the rule. The department has proposed applying regulations to a handful of countries — Singapore, Malaysia, Thailand, Indonesia, Brazil, South Africa and Norway. Others in the administration have wanted global coverage.

The proposal was first reported by The Information.

The Commerce Department proposal would also apply only to future shipments of advanced chips, exempting data centers already filled with American technology. Companies would need to notify the government if Chinese customers use their data centers to train A.I. models. But they would not automatically need to obtain a license.

The Commerce Department had also argued for the rules to kick in when companies are using a larger amount of computing power, meaning fewer activities by Chinese companies would be regulated.

Chris McGuire, a senior fellow at the Council on Foreign Relations and a former Biden administration official, predicted that Chinese companies would find ways to sidestep the more narrow controls the Commerce Department is proposing.

“If you’re only restricting remote access to data centers in certain countries, then China will just rent from the data centers outside those countries,” he said.

Nvidia had been one of Cantor’s largest stock positions early last year, but last fall, the firm began steadily selling off shares. Cantor holds those shares on behalf of clients, not as part of its proprietary investment portfolio.

Still, Cantor Fitzgerald continued to help arrange billions of dollars of financing for industries ranging from data centers to cryptocurrency that depend on a steady supply of computing from Nvidia.

That includes Bitdeer, which is building out the Malaysian data center it expects to generate $1.7 billion in revenue over five years, according to a company statement.

That data center will likely serve Tencent, a Chinese internet giant that would be able to gain access to Nvidia’s most advanced A.I. servers, according to a person with knowledge of the arrangement. Bitdeer is part of Nvidia’s partner network, a program for companies that work closely with the chipmaker.

Bitdeer hosts a Chinese language website that lets customers rent A.I. chips and gain access to Chinese open source A.I. models through data centers in Malaysia, Canada and elsewhere. The Johor facility is one of five data centers the company plans to open in Malaysia in the coming years, according to filings with the Securities and Exchange Commission.

Cantor holds a stake in Bitdeer through its investment in Tether, the crypto company. It is far from the only American financial heavyweight investing in overseas data centers. Bain Capital, Citadel and Blackstone have all poured money into A.I. computing clusters across the region.

Cantor also previously provided financial services to Gorilla Technology, which is building data centers in Thailand and Indonesia, and has a contract to provide A.I. computing to Freyr AI, a Singaporean data center firm that corporate filings and job ads indicate has ties to China.

Cantor has worked with other Nvidia partners globally, including IREN, an Australian cloud computing company, and Lancium, a Texas data center developer.

A Commerce Department spokeswoman said that Mr. Lutnick makes policy decisions based on the best interests of the United States. He does not discuss department matters with his sons, nor do they discuss Cantor Fitzgerald business with him, she added.

Cantor Fitzgerald declined to comment. Bitdeer did not reply to a request for comment.

Mr. Lutnick, as of October 2025, transferred his remaining ownership stake in Cantor to his family. Before that, he had been given what the White House had called a “limited waiver” that allowed him to participate in certain decisions that could have “a direct and predictable effect on Cantor Fitzgerald,” exempting him from a federal criminal law that would otherwise have required him to entirely recuse himself from these discussions.

Even after Mr. Lutnick finished transferring his ownership stake to his sons late last year, he still had to abide by an ethics rule prohibiting federal employees from using their public office for their private gain or the gain of friends and relatives.

The Times reported last year that Mr. Lutnick was promoting data center projects that worked with his family firms. Senator Elizabeth Warren, Democrat of Massachusetts, and two dozen other Democratic lawmakers called for an investigation.
